Dear all,

I am trying to analyze the sex differences in ontogenetic trajectories (infant, juvenile, subadult, adult)  in an anatomical structure of N=100 gorillas.

Here is the function that I used:

TA <- trajectory.analysis(coords~sex*ontogeny,data=gdf, iter=999)
summary(TA, angle.type = "deg")
plot(TA, group.cols = c("red", "green"),pt.seq.pattern = c("white","gray","black"),pt.scale = 1.5)

This is the resulting plot (with some modifications in Power Point):

This is the first time that I use this function so that I am not familiar with the outputs and interpretations. What I can interpret from this outline is that the trajectory in males seems to be longer than that of females. Also, the shape changes between juvenile and subadult in females are less pronounced than those in males because of the lenght of the vector. And also, changes between subadult and adult seem to follow different directions in males and females because the vectors are not paralell.

I have several questions on this:

1. What is the difference between this PCA and the PCA using plotTangentSpace()? In my case, this PCA shows 8 PCs and the common PCA shows 99 PC (N-1, as expected).
2. Is there any possibility to plot the trajectories along PC2-PC3?
3. Is there a way to represent my plot as in Figure 2B of the paper Adams, D. C., & Collyer, M. L. (2009). A general framework for the analysis of phenotypic trajectories in evolutionary studies. Evolution: International Journal of Organic Evolution, 63(5), 1143-1154.
3. I wonder whether my interpretations indicated below can be statistically confirmed by the outputs of the function. Among all the outputs, what should I focus on to know whether the trajectories in males and females are similar?  For example, here I show you some of the outputs that I have and my interpretation:

TA$path.distances
        F         M
0.4032812 0.5418699
Does this represent the distance between the starting point and the end point of the trajectories? Do these values mean that the distance is greater in males than in females (as can be observed in the plot)?

TA$trajectory.angle.deg
         F        M
F  0.00000 36.08188
M 36.08188  0.00000

What does this angle represent? Is there a way to calculate the angle between vectors, for example, angle between the vectors INFANT-JUVENILE in males and females? Does it make sense?

Sorry if these questions are discussed in a previous thread in this forum and I overlooked it (if so, please just let me know), and thank you very much in advance.

All the best,

Nicole

The PCA in this plot is based on the covariance matrix for trajectory points, not all points like in plotTangentSpace

> 2. Is there any possibility to plot the trajectories along PC2-PC3?

Not with the plotting of a trajectory.analysis object but you can extract the PC scores and plot them separately.  There is an object returned called $pca, which is a prcomp object; thus, $pca$x are the PC scores for each observation.  If pca = TRUE is used as an argument in the analysis (the default), the LS means that are returned are the trajectory points.  You can plot these in alternative dimensions.

> 3. Is there a way to represent my plot as in Figure 2B of the paper Adams, D. C., & Collyer, M. L. (2009). A general framework for the analysis of phenotypic trajectories in evolutionary studies. Evolution: International Journal of Organic Evolution, 63(5), 1143-1154.

Same as point 2 and choose a 3D plotting option, like those found in the rgl package.

> 3. I wonder whether my interpretations indicated below can be statistically confirmed by the outputs of the function. Among all the outputs, what should I focus on to know whether the trajectories in males and females are similar?  For example, here I show you some of the outputs that I have and my interpretation:
>
> TA$path.distances
>         F         M
> 0.4032812 0.5418699
> Does this represent the distance between the starting point and the end point of the trajectories?

Yes.

> Do these values mean that the distance is greater in males than in females (as can be observed in the plot)?

Yes

>
> TA$trajectory.angle.deg
>          F        M
> F  0.00000 36.08188
> M 36.08188  0.00000
>
> What does this angle represent?

The angle between principal vectors (first PC) of trajectories.

> Is there a way to calculate the angle between vectors, for example, angle between the vectors INFANT-JUVENILE in males and females?

Yes, if you wish to partition LS means to focus only on these vectors, the math is the same as calculating the vector correlation or angle between any two vectors.

Hope these responses help!  By the way, it looks like you are using an older version of trajectory.analysis.  My responses assume the most current version.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Raquel,

I find it curious that you got different results (the interaction Z-score and P-value should have been the same as the ANOVA between the two models), but let’s table that one for a moment.  The amount of variation explained by unique allometries is 3%.  The species differences account for 15% of the shape variation.  Nobody is obligated to choose a model based on a significance criterion if the effect size is small.  In your shoes, I would choose the common allometry model and compare species LS means (mean shape at mean size), not worrying about this little effect.  I think you are justified to say the a common allometry model is the model you want to work with.

Also, I would trust the anova(fit.unique) results and not the anova(fit.common, fit.unique).  Something is wrong there, and it seems emergent.  I will have to debug that code.  So thank you for your example, as it found a problem!

Finally, the anova(fit.size, fit.species) result you found was much more impressive because the former model has one slope, the latter model has each species intercept and unique slope, meaning it confounds species means and slopes.  Of course there is a significant difference because species means are different (but you cannot tell it is that or slopes without further investigation).  You now know species means are different and allometric variation does not complicate this inference.

Hope that helps!
Mike

Dear All,

I have a couple of questions regarding the use of the Kmult statistic included in the "physignal" function of the geomorph package for estimating phylogenetic signal using high-dimension multivariate traits.

I computed the Kmulti statistic for my shape data (3D landmarks/semilandmarks for three different bones in six taxa) and obtained non-significant p-values: bone 1 K = 0.61 p = 0.07; bone 2 K = 0.32 p = 0.38 and bone 3 K = 0.55, p = 0.66

Thus, I´m wondering if the lack of statistical significance could be also related to my small sample size (n=6 taxa) and if I can say, according to the results, that despite of the lack of statistical significance the bone 1 has a stronger phylogenetic signal than bones 2 and 3; and that the bone 3 has a stronger phylogenetic signal than bone 2.

Thank in advance for some information.

All the best,

Paolo

Paolo,

To add to what Antigoni stated, yes: this is absolutely related to sample size. Recall that significance is derived from permutation, so with N=6 there are only a few combinatoric possibilities of random outcome.

As to your other question (is there ‘stronger’ signal in one versus the other component?), one could infer this as you have. However, a far better way to go is to use an empirically-derive effect size (Z-score) and compare these. We do this in geomorph to obtain the z-scores in linear models; the procedure is described in Collyer, Sekora, and Adams 2015 Heredity.  A related approach is found in Adams and Collyer 2016 for comparing levels of integration across datasets.

Essentially, the effect size is:

Z = (Stat_obs – Mean_rand)  / std_rand

Where ‘rand’ refers to the empirical sampling distribution under permutation.

Dean

# This gives 1 x 2 array with coordinates ~1e-17, rather than 12 x 2 array

# Count number of species
p.sp.list <- levels(factor(plethodon$species))
# Create temporary landmark array to place species means into
p.sp.coords.means <- p.gpa$coords[,,1:length(p.sp.list)]

# Calculate mean lm configuration for each species using loop
for (i in 1:length(p.sp.list)) {
   p.sp.coords.means[,,i] <- mshape(p.gpa$coords[,,plethodon$species ==
p.sp.list[i]])

levels(p.sp3) <- c(levels(factor(plethodon$species)), c("New"))

p.sp3.list <- levels(factor(p.sp3))

# Create temporary landmark array to place species means into
p.sp3.coords.means <- p.gpa$coords[,,1:length(p.sp3.list)]

# Calculate mean lm configuration for three species
for (i in 1:length(p.sp3.list)) {

without using a loop, so I would be very grateful for suggestions for
that. However, the mshape appears to give an incorrect result even
without the loop.

If anyone has suggestions for what I might be doing wrong please let me
know.

Al

messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph community,

Based on this thread, I have updated the mshape function to distinguish between two matrices: one that is a single specimen and one that is an n x pk matrix, where rows are specimens and columns are coordinates; i.e., 1x, 1y, 1z, 2x, 2y, 2z, …

This was possible by checking the dimensions of the matrix.  If a matrix (specifically, a 2D array) comprises the data and the number of columns is 2 or 3, it is assumed that this is a single specimen and mshape returns the coordinates of the one specimen.  (It is possible that somebody digitized exactly one point for multiple specimens, and then arranged the data into a matrix instead of a 3D array, but we will have to risk this as a rare exception… and/or question the logic.)  If a matrix has more than 3 columns, and it can be assumed specimens are rows, then the function returns column means.

The update is currently made to the Github version of geomorph.  For multiple specimen arrays, you should notice no change to the function.  This should alleviate any sorting issues that cull a data set into a single specimen, when finding means by groups.

Thanks to Murat Maga for pointing out a logical redundancy in our code!

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Yes this can be done.   The trick is to give shape.predictor the PLS scores directly, rather than asking it to compute them (when it computes, it uses PLS1 as per the help file).

This is the standard approach for PLS-1

preds <- shape.predictor(Y.gpa$coords, plethShapeFood$food, Intercept = FALSE,

                         method = "PLS", pred1 = 2, pred2 = -4, pred3 = 2.5) # using PLS plot as a guide

Here is the approach for PLS-2: NOTE: one must perform the PLS ahead of time, and provide the scores from that.

preds2 <- shape.predictor(Y.gpa$coords, PLS$XScores[,2], Intercept = FALSE,

                         method = "LS", pred1 = 2, pred2 = -4, pred3 = 2.5) # using PLS plot as a guide

Notice also that one changes method to ‘LS’ rather than ‘PLS’ because the PLS was pre-computed.

As to your last question, determining meaningful values for the predicted shapes is a case-by-case basis. For a continuous variable, we often look towards the extremes of our data distribution along the regression or correlation plot. To do this, one must identify them via visual inspection, as you correct determined was the case for the two extremes used in the example. There is not an automatic way for this at present: human intervention is required, and in fact encouraged, as only the researcher knows what they wish to plot!

What if you perform ANOVA on fit.full?

anova(fit.full)

I am willing to bet the interaction term is not significant.  Your pairwise test - without providing a specific null model - will use the one inherent in fit full.  This can be revealed with

Mike

preds2 <- shape.predictor(Y.gpa$coords, PLS$YScores[,3], Intercept = FALSE,

                         method = "LS", pred1 = min(PLS$YScores[,3]), pred2 = max(PLS$YScores[,3])) # using PLS plot as a guide

preds3 <- shape.predictor(Y.gpa$coords, PLS$XScores[,2], Intercept = FALSE,

messages.body_plain:
Marla,

the sliders definition matrix only needs to be made once, as it is the same set of landmarks that will be sliding during GPA for ALL specimens. Note that this matrix is just a table that defines which landmarks slide between which other two, with one slider per line. So, a line saying e.g. 5, 6, 7 says "landmark 6 is a semilandmark that will slide between 5 and 7", a definition that will be the same for all individuals. As you mentioned define.sliders, I am assuming here that you are taking about curve NOT SURFACE semilandmarks. If you also have semilandmarks on surfaces, you need to put their numbers into a vector to be used with the argument "surfaces" in gpagen.

As for the landmark coordinates, yes, you will need to compile those into a single object, e.g. by writing a loop to read all of your coordinate csv files and compile them into a 3d array. Then your GPA would be something like:

my.gpa.result <- gpagen(mycoords, curves = semi.definition.matrix, surfaces = semi.definition.vector)

Again, all semilandmarks are the same for all specimens, so they only need to be defined once.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tobias,

> a) how can I identify (or label)  the two modules  in the combined data set.  'T' and 'C'  are two bones from the same individual.   T was landmarked with  124   3D landmarks and C  was described with   116   3D landmarks.   I guess my  use of the  rep    function is incorrect.

partition.gp <http://partition.gp> <- c(rep(“T”, 124), rep(“C”, 116))
>
> b) 'T' and 'C'   have been independently landmarked.  Is the  modularity.test    function appropriate to test for  modularity between the two bones?  (Eventually I intend to include more than those  2 bones.)

This is a good question, which provokes two responses for me.  First, if this is legitimate, I think that in combining subsets, if GPA is preformed and both subsets are aligned to principal axes, it should be okay.  Second, is it legitimate?  These are separate bones.  Although one might want to use both to characterize morphology, are they not already completely modular by being separate?  Are they dermal skull bones that are sutured to compose one structure?  In other words, it seems a little silly to take two separate bones - e.g., a humerus and a femur - and ask if there is modularity, because of course there is if they are different structures, altogether.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Dear Tobias,

Further to what Mike has already said, another option would be to use ShapeRotator (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ece3.4018). This R tool is basically the 3D-equivalent of Adams’ (1999) fixed.angle function for 2D-data.

ShapeRotator removes the effect of random translations and rotations across specimens by rotating the landmarks of each structure to a predefined angle. So, for example, 3D landmarks from a humerus and radioulna could be placed at 90 degrees relative to one another before performing a GPA. In principle, you should be able to add as many bones or modules as you want.

Even though ShapeRotator was designed for articulated structures, it can also be used as a method for bringing any integrated (e.g. functionally-integrated but not necessarily connected) anatomical structures into a shared 3D-space, with standardised positions and angles between them.

In this paper we used ShapeRotator for single-point articulations (e.g. humerus - radioulna, femur – tibiofibula, and also all four limb bones together): https://bmcevolbiol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12862-017-0993-0

And Kazi & Hipsley (2018) used it for double-point articulations (crania and mandibles), which had been independently landmarked: https://academic.oup.com/biolinnean/article-abstract/125/1/14/5053605

If you decide to use ShapeRotator: I would expect some differences in Procrustes coordinates between the combined.subset function in geomorph and ShapeRotator, but there would also be differences when using different angles in ShapeRotator, so a biologically meaningful angle is best.

Kind regards,

Marta

messages.body_plain:
RD,

Presently, geomorph does not allow for additional factors in the bilat.symmetry model. In theory this can be done with more general code; and in fact it is on the list of possible upgrades for a future version of geomorph. But we presently don’t only allow for a single additional factor, as in our view that is limiting (why not 2 factors? Interactions, etc.?). We prefer implementing fully flexible statistical approaches, but devising this for the case of symmetry is not trivial. This is why the additional factor (as in MorphoJ) is not currently in bilat.symmetry.

Thus at present you have two options. First, one could run the bilat.symmetry as you have done, extract the FA component and then run a comparison of groups on the FA component. Here you are able to compare levels of FA among groups, but not in the context of the full symmetry analysis. This may be less desirable because in this case the variation among groups is not evaluated relative to the rest of the model (whether or not that is an issue is something one could discuss).

The second option is more involved. Basically, one can run a linear model on the data using procD.lm, and include the requisite components for DA and FA.  However, doing so will require replicating some of the underlying code in bilat.symmetry to up-front extract the DA and FA components properly.  Not easy if one is an R-novice, but it is possible to do.
